entry.title: A comparative approach to the evolution of kissing

link.title: A comparative approach to the evolution of kissing

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 6

The 2026 Igs were held a couple weeks ago, I wanted a fun lighthearted read today, so I decided to read one of the winning papers. The prize was awarded for devising a more precise definition of kissing – “non-agonistic interactions involving directed, intraspecific, oral-oral contact with some movement of the lips/mouthparts and no food transfer” – in ants, birds, polar bears, and humans. The definition is indeed the most interesting part of the paper, as most of the rest was a plea for more data. They also did some complicated Monte Carlo Markov Chain modelling to predict whether kissing is an ancestral trait for Afro-Eurasian monkeys and apes, but I’m not sure the results are super trustworthy considering the sparcity of data. Although, I don’t know anything about how these evolution models work, should probably read up on them, they sound like they have interesting maths.

entry.title: Electron Radiated Power in Cyclotron Radiation Emission Spectroscopy Experiments

link.title: Electron Radiated Power in Cyclotron Radiation Emission Spectroscopy Experiments

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 6

Truth be told, today’s paper was pretty dang hard for me to read. If you’ve read anything complicated ever, you know how it is: you see some topic mentioned that you are unfamiliar with, so you go search for it, and its explanation references something else you don’t know, so you go research that, etc. So I ended up going through the derivation of Liénard–Wiechert fields, then the Larmor formula, and only then went back to the paper. That helped. A little bit.

The paper itself is about figuring out initial kinetic energy distribution of electrons by looking at the radiation they spew out while trapped in a waveguide in a “magnetic bottle”. The coolest part is for sure that the magnetobremsstrahlung’s spectrum in this case looks like a comb of equidistant delta functions, separated by axial frequency. That is the result of a LOT of Fourier transform magic that I could barely follow (because there’s like three different periodic motions happening at the same time).

All this electron whirling and twirling I read, while listening to Debussy’s String Quartet in G minor and the album called “Sounds of atoms” by Sayer (found thanks to the track called Cyclotron, for obvious reasons). Y’know what, I say scientists should compile soundtracks for their papers, just like TTRPG players do for their characters. Would science be better off for it? No idea, prolly not. But it sure as heck would be fun!

entry.title: On the Law of Distribution of Energy in the Normal Spectrum

link.title: On the Law of Distribution of Energy in the Normal Spectrum

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 5

Today I spent reviewing blackbody radiation laws, hence this paper. I first read Planck’s 1900 paper (I strongly suspect it is rather a lecture transcript), and it’s literally just “I love Wien’s law, I find it beautiful, but it’s sadly kinda wrong for large wavelengths. So I tinkered with a ton of expressions similar to Wien’s law, and look at the cool formula I found as a result. It works really well, idk why” (not a quote). In contrast, the 1901 paper is basically the same as what we do in intro to stat mech while deriving Bose-Einstein distribution, just without the chemical potential. And also with Wien’s displacement law postulated (not the same as Wien’s law (which is really an approximation), because that’s not confusing at all), together with a discretisation of vibrational energy. A bit annoying to read due to the aforementioned displacement law being presented as a relationship between energy density and wavelength, which I was unfamiliar with, but ultimately not particularly different from how we did it in uni. What did surprise me, though, was that this paper is where the \(E=h\nu\) is derived, and it is derived from the Wien’s displacement law!

entry.title: Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid

link.title: Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 4

The reason today’s paper is what it is – it’s surprisingly short, just a tiny bit longer than a single page, and I was lazy today. Despite having spent four years in uni studying bio, I never bothered to even search for this particular historical paper before. It’s a nice read, gives a bit more perspective on the history of the discovery. The fact that they actually openly acknowledged being influenced by unpublished research by Wilkins and Franklin was a tad surprising to me. The story as told in books and movies has Watson and Crick accessing that research by semi-clandestine means, but after reading the paper I wonder what actually happened…

entry.title: A simple derivation for the skin effect in a round wire

link.title: A simple derivation for the skin effect in a round wire

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 3

Today’s paper is my admission of defeat. First, I tried reading Horace Lamb’s original 1883 paper, but after like four pages I had to drop it. Not only does he operate in components of vectors, and writes triples of equations for everything, rather than use vector identities, like a sane person, he also gives each component a SEPARATE LETTER… I’m not fuming, you’re fuming!

Anyway, this paper is from the European counterpart to yesterday’s journal, so the derivation is meant to be comprehensible by an undergraduate student. I’m kinda disappointed in that, because the author decided that an undergraduate student should be more familiar with the integral formulations of Maxwell equations than the differential ones, and that solving an integral equation would be easier for them than a PDE… I’m sure for some people that is indeed the case, but I’ve always found the differential forms (yes, pun intended) cleaner and easier work with. And yes, this derivation is nice, yielding an equation for current in terms of its own double integral, which is solved by iteratively plugging \(J_{i-1}\) into the expression for \(J_i\). But the resulting solution is a series, and I don’t have the analysis prowess required to recognise the Bessel function in that mess. Dunno why the author thought it would be simpler than using vector identities…

entry.title: The Bounce of a Ball
entry.content:
A paper a day: day 2

Today’s paper comes from the journal that I discovered only last week, but it’s quickly becoming one of my favourites. “American Journal of Physics”, despite the grandiose name, is actually created by and for physics teachers, and hence most articles are hyper readable and approachable by a much more general audience than in your average bleeding-edge journal. I’ve honestly just started browsing it randomly, and every article I read felt easily digestible, like sci-comm. Could really eat them like candy :-p

This particular paper pertains to the physics of bouncing balls: the author dropped them onto a piezo plate and recorded how normal force changes during the bounce. Very nice and simple experimental setup, could feasibly be reproduced in the classroom, which, I’m guessing, is the whole point of this journal.

entry.title: The Schrödinger Two-Electron Atomic Problem
entry.content:
A paper a day: day 1

Today’s paper is about the issues that arose when the old quantum theory met with the three body problem that is a helium atom, and the ways it was ultimately solved. This is not one of the original 1928-1929 Hylleraas papers – those ones are in German, and I didn’t want to bother. No, this is better: it’s a paper (a book chapter, really), written by Hylleraas himself almost thirty years after the fact, overviewing the problem and the advances in the field that happened since then. The chapter uses techniques very familiar to someone who has studied QM in a modern university, to me it was kinda surprising, and very welcome. It was also cool to witness how the Hylleraas coordinates (sum of electrons’ distances to the nucleus, their difference, and the distance between the electrons themselves) are so simple, yet so effective. With the amount of different stuff they tried, I’m really surprised this is what worked. I also chuckled every time there were references like “this has been used with considerable success by Hylleraas (1932)” (and boy, were there a lot of them). Scientists citing themselves in the third person will never stop being funny…
